performers: John Harrison, violin; Wichita State University Chamber Players; Robert Turizziani, conductor
intro: The solo violin sits by the fire while the orchestral violins make rain against the window. Vivaldi writes the raindrops pizzicato and forte, with the bass kept quiet beneath them.

sections.label: A · A violin by the fire
sections.mNote: Bowed solo above plucked violins and a quiet bass

sections.label: A′ · The melody starts from B♭
sections.mNote: The opening tune returns in B♭ and works towards E♭

sections.label: Coda · E♭ held above the rain
sections.mNote: The solo sustains E♭ while the plucked violins continue

cues.title: Indoors by the fire
cues.text: “Passar al foco i dì quieti e contenti” — “To spend the days by the fire, peaceful and content.” The 1725 sonnet brings us indoors. The solo violin sings in E♭ major over plucked violin notes; the bass is marked always quiet.
cues.evidence: Winter sonnet, letter E; translation ours. Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles, II, opening bars, bass marked Sempre Piano: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351. Italian text also at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Four_Seasons_(Vivaldi).
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Rain outside the window
cues.text: “Mentre la pioggia fuor bagna ben cento” — “While outside the rain soaks a hundred others.” The orchestral violins pluck their raindrops throughout. After its first cadence in B♭ major, the solo melody starts again from B♭ and bends its way back towards E♭.
cues.evidence: Winter sonnet, 1725, letter E; translation ours. Italian text at https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/36996; Mutopia score, II, bars 8–16, with La Pioggia and Pizziccati forte in the orchestral violins.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The melody settles on E♭
cues.text: The solo violin reaches E♭ and holds it through the last bars. Below, the rain keeps falling in plucked semiquavers. Only at the final fermata do the orchestral violins stop their patter and hold the chord.
cues.evidence: Mutopia score, II, bars 16–18: the solo E♭ is tied across the closing bars, and the orchestral violin semiquavers end at the final fermata: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=351.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: The tune starts again on B♭
transitions.from: A · A violin by the fire
transitions.to: A′ · The melody starts from B♭
transitions.how: The solo’s C trill resolves to B♭ at the end of the first eight bars. The melody begins again on B♭, a fourth below its original E♭. Plucked violins and the quiet bass continue underneath; the altered second half leads back to E♭ major.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, II, bars 7–16; the two-phrase design is described at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2022/vivaldi-seasons/inverno/02.php.

transitions.title: The solo holds above the raindrops
transitions.from: A′ · The melody starts from B♭
transitions.to: Coda · E♭ held above the rain
transitions.how: The solo’s D rises to E♭ and stays there. The orchestral violins continue plucking E♭-major arpeggios beneath the held note before the final fermata. The bowed melody comes to rest while the raindrops still move.

source.title: Vivaldi, The Four Seasons — Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles
source.locator: II. Largo, all 18 bars; stable bowed-solo / pizzicato-violin / quiet-bass texture. Passage-level participation, not individual attack alignment; cellos/basses represent the written basso part, with no claim about keyboard realization.

timeline.note: The solo violin sings above plucked orchestral violins and quieter accompanying strings; the diagram describes the movement’s stable texture, not uninterrupted activity in every part.

composer.epithet: He wrote concertos for the women of Venice’s Pietà, operas for its theatres, and a barking dog for the viola.
facts: Violin with his father Giovanni Battista, a player at St Mark’s, Venice
Pietà violin teacher from 1703; maestro de’ concerti from 1716; court service in Mantua, 1718–20
More than 500 concertos, operas, sacred music and sonatas
composer.background:
In 1703 a twenty-five-year-old Venetian became a priest in March and a violin teacher in September. Antonio Vivaldi had red hair, a formidable bow arm and a chest complaint that made celebrating Mass difficult. His father Giovanni Battista had been a barber before joining the violinists at St Mark’s; he taught Antonio and continued helping with his career long after the son had become famous. Venice knew Antonio as il prete rosso, the red priest. His working places would be the chapel, the orchestra gallery and the opera house.

The Ospedale della Pietà cared for abandoned children. Its musical establishment was a selected group of girls and women, trained to sing and play to a standard that brought visitors from across Europe. Some remained there as adult musicians and teachers. Vivaldi taught the advanced string players, rehearsed the orchestra and supplied new pieces. The governors voted on his employment each year: in 1709 they dispensed with him, and in 1711 took him back. The music survived the office politics.
